Born in New York on April 22, 1904, J. Robert Oppenheimer led the development and construction of the world's first atomic weapons. Educated at Harvard, Cambridge, and the University of Gottingen, Oppenheimer taught physics in California before embarking on his role in the Manhattan Project as the director of the top-secret Los Alamos Laboratory. After the war, his past communist leanings came to a head when his government security clearance was revoked after several contentious hearings at the height of the "Red Scare".

Born in New York on April 22, 1904, J. Robert Oppenheimer led the development and construction of the world's first atomic weapons. Educated at Harvard, Cambridge, and the University of Gottingen, Oppenheimer taught physics in California before embarking on his role in the Manhattan Project as the director of the top-secret Los Alamos Laboratory. After the war, his past communist leanings came to a head when his government security clearance was revoked after several contentious hearings at the height of the "Red Scare".

J. Robert Oppenheimer (full name: Julius Robert Oppenheimer; April 22, 1904 – February 18, 1967) was born in New York City, USA. He held a doctorate and was a Jewish-American physicist, a member of the National Academy of Sciences, the leader of the Manhattan Project, and served as the director of the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, USA, until his death.
4
J. Robert Oppenheimer entered the Ethical Culture Fieldston School for his studies, completing the third and fourth grades in one year. He graduated early from Harvard University in 1925 and went to study at the Cavendish Laboratory at the University of Cambridge that same year. In 1926, he transferred to Germany for further study. He earned his doctorate from the Georg-August-Universität Göttingen in 1927. He returned to the United States in 1929 and began teaching at the University of California, Berkeley. He was elected a member of the National Academy of Sciences in 1941. In 1942, he was appointed the chief scientist of the 'Manhattan Project' for developing the atomic bomb. In 1943, he oversaw the establishment of the Los Alamos National Laboratory and served as its director. After World War II ended in 1945, he began teaching at the California Institute of Technology. He served as director of the Institute for Advanced Study from 1947 to 1966. His security clearance was revoked in 1954. He died of throat cancer on February 18, 1967, at the age of 62. On December 16, 2022, the 1954 decision to revoke J. Robert Oppenheimer's security clearance was overturned.
2
J. Robert Oppenheimer worked in theoretical physics, including research and leadership in Quantum mechanics and nuclear physics. He made contributions in theoretical astronomy, nuclear physics, spectroscopy, and quantum field theory (including quantum electrodynamics). Together with Max Born, he proposed the Born–Oppenheimer approximation for describing molecular wave functions. He received awards including the Presidential Medal for Merit and the Enrico Fermi Award.

Biography
Early Life
On April 22, 1904, J. Robert Oppenheimer was born in
New York City
, United States, into a wealthy German-Jewish family. In his early years, he explored fields such as literature, philosophy, and languages. He was initially educated at Alcuin Preparatory School, and then attended the Ethical Culture Fieldston School. There he completed the third and fourth grades in one year and skipped one semester of the eighth grade.
2
In 1921, he graduated from Fieldston School with straight A's in ten subjects. In the same year, his entry into university was delayed by a year after he contracted colitis during a family vacation in
Czechoslovakia
and subsequently underwent recuperation in
New Mexico
.
In 1922, he entered Harvard College to study chemistry. During his undergraduate years, he was admitted to the Phi Beta Kappa honor society and qualified for graduate studies in physics based on independent study.
32
In 1925, he graduated early from Harvard College with honors. In the same year, he went to the
University of Cambridge
for further studies, hoping to conduct experimental physics research under
Ernest Rutherford
. However, Ernest Rutherford was unwilling to accept him as a student, so he began to study theoretical physics instead, joining the
Cavendish Laboratory
under the tutelage of
Joseph John Thomson
.
In 1927, he graduated from the University of Göttingen with a doctorate in physics. For the next two years, he conducted further research successively in
Zurich

, Switzerland, and Leiden, Netherlands.
Career Experience
In the summer of 1929, after returning to the United States, he contracted tuberculosis and recuperated at a ranch near the town of Los Alamos, New Mexico; in the same year, he began teaching at the
University of California, Berkeley
, and founded the "Oppenheimer Center for Theoretical Physics".
In 1941, he was elected a member of the National Academy of Sciences.
Oppenheimer and Chen-Ning Yang
In August 1942, he was appointed the chief scientist of the "Manhattan Project" to develop the atomic bomb.
In 1943, he oversaw the establishment of the Los Alamos Laboratory in the New Mexico desert and served as its director, with
Edward Teller
assisting J. Robert Oppenheimer in organizing the team working at Los Alamos.
3
In July 1945, he led the effort that produced the world's first atomic bomb; in October, he resigned as director of the Los Alamos Laboratory and subsequently taught briefly at the
California Institute of Technology
.
30
In 1954, his security clearance was revoked by the Atomic Energy Commission (AEC).

In 1966, he retired from the
Institute for Advanced Study
and was soon diagnosed with throat cancer.
30
On February 18, 1967, he died of throat cancer in Princeton, New Jersey, United States, at the age of 62. He was cremated, and his ashes were scattered over the
The British Virgin Islands
.

Major Achievements
Scientific Achievements
*   Research Overview
J. Robert Oppenheimer made contributions across several fields including theoretical astronomy, nuclear physics, spectroscopy, and quantum field theory (including quantum electrodynamics). Together with Max Born, he proposed the Born–Oppenheimer approximation for describing molecular wave functions.
23

Oppenheimer's initial research focus was on the theory of continuous spectra. His first published paper in 1926 was on the quantum theory of molecular band spectra. He devised a method for calculating transition probabilities between energy levels, applied it to the photoelectric effect of hydrogen emitting X-rays, and calculated the absorption coefficient for the K-edge. The calculations for hydrogen matched the solar X-ray absorption spectrum, but those for helium did not. It was only discovered years later that the sun is primarily composed of hydrogen, meaning his calculations had been correct all along.
24
Oppenheimer did some work on the theory of cosmic rays and initiated work describing quantum tunneling. In 1931, together with his student Harvey Hall, he published "On the Quantum Theory of the Photoelectric Effect," which correctly refuted, based on experimental evidence, Dirac's assertion that two energy levels of the hydrogen atom were degenerate.
25
Oppenheimer and his doctoral student Melba Phillips performed calculations on artificial radioactivity produced by deuteron bombardment. In 1935, they developed a more powerful new theory known as the Oppenheimer–Phillips process.
26
In 1930, Oppenheimer pointed out that the "holes" in P.A.M. Dirac's electron theory were not protons but should be a new positively charged particle with the same mass as the electron, thus predicting the existence of the positron.
39
In late 1930, J. Robert Oppenheimer began researching astrophysics. In 1938, he co-authored a paper with Robert Serber titled "On the Stability of Stellar Neutron Cores," which explored the properties of white dwarfs. Subsequently, in a paper with his student George Volkoff, "On Massive Neutron Cores," he demonstrated that stable neutron stars have a certain mass limit; once exceeded, gravitational collapse would occur, leading to what is known as the Tolman–Oppenheimer–Volkoff limit. In 1939, with his student Hartland Snyder, he published "On Continued Gravitational Attraction," predicting the existence of black holes.
